newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-LVMH stays mum on GrandMet remarks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-LVMH stays mum on GrandMet remarks.

text.p: LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton said on Thursday that it was still awaiting a formal response to its chairman's proposal to create a three-way drinks merger with GrandMet and Guinness.
An LVMH spokeswoman also declined to comment on remarks by Grand Metropolitan chief executive John McGrath that such a three-way drinks deal could be reached this year if benefits were fairly shared.
LVMH Chairman Bernard Arnault put his case to institutional investors in London on Thursday. "We are waiting for the final answer from Guinness and GrandMet," the spokeswoman said.
LVMH has enough shares in GrandMet -- 11.06 percent -- to call an extraordinary general meeting to present his proposal if the Guinness and GrandMet chairmen, as expected, reject his plan next week.
One analyst said the outcome of the boardroom fight would be decided by the GrandMet shareholders. LVMH is the biggest one today. If it can put together a 25 percent block, it can stop the deal.
"If push comes to shove, Arnault will liquidate his (12.3 percent) Guinness holding to buy GrandMet," said the analyst, who estimates Arnault could end up with as much as 20 percent of GrandMet.
Arnault is focusing on GrandMet because he needs an outright majority at Guinness to block the deal.
McGrath, in remarks published in the Financial Times, rejected Arnault's view that more value would be generated if the British groups demerged their food, fast-food and brewing activities.
McGrath was quoted as saying that exhaustive analysis showed that the value of the parts did not exceed that of the whole.
He also said that, as Arnault was now set to hold about 12 percent of the new company formed by the British groups' merger, GMG Brands, he should have a proportional benefit of the merger benefits.
McGrath said a combination of the drinks businesses within GMG Brands was an attractive possibility.
But Arnault, who indirectly holds 25 percent of LVMH and controls more than 40 percent, does not want LVMH capital locked up in a GMG subsidiary.
He wants a separate, listed drinks groups in which Arnault would be the dominant shareholder with a stake estimated at around 30 percent.

McGrath, who is chief executive designate of GMG, told The Independent newspaper, "It is our clear intention to find some form of settlement between the sides." But he said it appeared Arnault's proposals were still not acceptable.
The Independent also said GrandMet would consider another possibility, that of splitting Moet Hennessy, 66 percent owned by LVMH and 34 percent by Guinness, into two units -- champagnes and cognacs.
LVMH declined to comment on that possibility.
Arnault is expected to make more trips like Thursday's to talk to investors. The more backing he gets, the less he has to spend buying GrandMet stock.
LVMH did not say who Arnault met on Thursday.

But the French newspaper La Tribune, owned by one of Arnault's companies, said he was expected to meet with managers at a big U.S. bank and possibly Mercury Asset Management, which has sold around half its 5.08 percent stake in GrandMet to LVMH.
Other investors include Schroder Investment Management with 2.2 percent, BGI with 2.7 percent, Prudential with 4.7 percent and Norwich Union wiht two percent, according to French media reports.
